title: NCSA Mosaic → Netscape
summary: NCSA Mosaic was a graphical web browser built in 1993 by students and staff at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA) at the University of Illinois, which NSF says grew out of NSF-funded research. In April 1994 Jim Clark and Marc Andreessen, one of Mosaic's developers, incorporated Mosaic Communications, which hired much of the Mosaic team and was renamed Netscape after the university objected; the dispute was settled in December 1994. The university licensed the exclusive commercial rights to NCSA Mosaic to a different company, Spyglass, not to Netscape. NCSA kept developing Mosaic until January 1997, so the tie between the public program and Netscape is people, not a transfer of code or rights.

links.claim: Marc Andreessen developed web-browsing software while working at NCSA at the University of Illinois, then co-founded Mosaic Communications (later Netscape) with Jim Clark in 1994.
Eric Bina, an NCSA programmer who developed the first working version of Mosaic with Andreessen in 1993, co-founded Netscape; the new company hired Bina and much of the Mosaic team.

claims.claim: Netscape was NCSA Mosaic commercialized under license from the University of Illinois.
claims.explanation: Spyglass's annual report states that in May 1994 the University of Illinois granted Spyglass the exclusive right to develop, distribute and sublicense commercial products based on NCSA Mosaic, in exchange for royalties. Netscape's own 10-K lists NCSA Mosaic, distributed free for noncommercial use, as a competing product. The tie to Netscape is the developers who moved, not a license.

claims.claim: Netscape's founders took Mosaic from the University of Illinois.
claims.explanation: The university claimed Andreessen had taken Mosaic and demanded a name change. The dispute was settled on December 21, 1994: the company became Netscape and the university received a financial settlement, which with legal costs cost Netscape close to $3 million. No court ruled on the claim, and the settlement is not an admission.
